"Dai Dai" (lit. 'Come on, come on') is a song by Colombian singer [Shakira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakira) and Nigerian singer [Burna Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burna_Boy). It was released on 15 May 2026, through Ace Entertainment and [Sony Music Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music_Latin) as [the official song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_FIFA_World_Cup_songs_and_anthems) for the [2026 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_FIFA_World_Cup) held in the United States, Mexico, and Canada.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Billboard1-1) It mentions several notable football players, such as [Pelé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelé), [Diego Maradona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Maradona), [Cristiano Ronaldo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cristiano_Ronaldo), [Lionel Messi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Messi), [Kylian Mbappé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kylian_Mbappé), and [Mohamed Salah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Salah).[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-3)
Commercially, the song become the fourth FIFA World Cup track to chart on the [Billboard Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100), and the highest-charting official FIFA World Cup song in [UK chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Charts) history.[\[A\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-5) The song also peaked at number one in Argentina, Austria, Belgium, Colombia, Czech Republic, Ecuador, France, Germany, Greece, Iceland, India, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Sweden, Switzerland, and United Arab Emirates as well as within the top three in Canada, Ireland, Spain, Singapore, and the UK.
Background and release
[
[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dai_Dai&action=edit§ion=1)]
On 7 May 2026, Shakira posted a short video on her [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram) account which featured the singer holding the [official soccer ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adidas_Trionda) of the 2026 FIFA World Cup on the football field of [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro)'s [Maracanã Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maracanã_Stadium), announcing the song and its title.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-6) On 14 May 2026, it was announced that Shakira, [Madonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madonna), and [K-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-pop) group [BTS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BTS) would co-headline the FIFA's first final halftime show on 19 July 2026, at [MetLife Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetLife_Stadium) in [East Rutherford, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Rutherford,_New_Jersey).[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-7)
The song was first released on 15 May 2026 in full audio, followed by the release of the song's music video on 23 May 2026.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-8) The song marks the fourth official [FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup) song performed by Shakira and the first since "[Dare (La La La)](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dare_(La_La_La)>)" for the [2014 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_FIFA_World_Cup) in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil).[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-9) The song is also the official anthem of the [Global Citizen](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Citizen_(organization)>) Fund for Education of the 2026 FIFA World Cup to ensure that children around the world have readily available access to quality education and sporting activities.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-10) A Spanish-language version of the song was released on 23 June 2026.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-11)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-12)
Composition
[
[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dai_Dai&action=edit§ion=2)]
The song was written by Shakira and Burna Boy, together with Benny Adam, [Jon Bellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Bellion), [Ed Sheeran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Sheeran), and Alexander Castillo, who produced the song with Shakira. The song was written in five languages: [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language), [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language), [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language), [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language), and [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language).[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:0-13) Its musical influences include [Afrobeats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrobeats), [dance-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance-pop), [world music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music), and [reggaeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggaeton).[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:1-14)
The title of the song, "Dai Dai", is in Italian and is a slang exclamation meaning "come on", an exhortation to "give it your all" in a sporting performance.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:0-13)
Critical reception
[
[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dai_Dai&action=edit§ion=3)]
[Billboard](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_(magazine)>) listed the song as the third-best song for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, stating that it "blends the musical worlds" of the two artists, with "the artists send a motivational and uplifting message to athletes and fans alike".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:1-14) Marni Rose McFall of [Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek) described the song as "a massive, rhythm‑driven anthem" praising "Shakira's unmistakable flair" and "Burna Boy's [Afro fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro_fusion) mastery".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-15)

Commercial performance
[
[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dai_Dai&action=edit§ion=5)]
"Dai Dai" has reached and stayed at number one on the [Billboard Global 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Global_200) for seven non-consecutive weeks (including four consecutive weeks),[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-18) becoming Shakira's second number-one song on the chart, after "[TQG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TQG)" with [Karol G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karol_G) in 2023, and Burna Boy's first one.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-19) The song also peaked at number one on several international charts, including Argentina, Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Lebanon, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Sweden, and United Arab Emirates, and within the top five in Ireland, Spain, and the UK. 
In the United States, "Dai Dai" debuted at number 75 on the [Billboard Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100), becoming the fourth official World Cup song to appear on the chart and making Shakira the first artist to have two official anthems appear on the chart, along with "[Waka Waka (This Time for Africa)](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waka_Waka_(This_Time_for_Africa)>)" from [2010 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_FIFA_World_Cup).[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-20) Following the World Cup final, the song peaked at number 17 on the chart dated 1 August 2026, becoming the highest-charting FIFA World Cup anthem in Billboard Hot 100 history.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:2-21) The song also peaked at number one on the [Billboard Latin Airplay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Airplay), extending Shakira's record for the most number-one songs on the chart for a female artist at 25.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-22)
In the United Kingdom, "Dai Dai" debuted at number 87 on the [Official Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_singles_chart) on 18 June 2026. In its seventh week on the chart, the song reached number five,[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-23) becoming Shakira's seventh song to enter the top ten, the first since "[She Wolf](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/She_Wolf_(Shakira_song)>)" peaked at number four in 2009,[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:3-24) and Burna Boy's fifth top ten song.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-25) Following the World Cup final, the song peaked at number two for two consecutive weeks behind [Sam Fender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Fender) and [Olivia Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivia_Dean)'s collaboration "[Rein Me In](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rein_Me_In)".[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-26) It became Shakira's highest placement on the UK Singles Chart since "[Beautiful Liar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beautiful_Liar)" with [Beyoncé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyoncé) in 2007.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:3-24)
In Australia, "Dai Dai" reached the top ten for the week ending 31 July 2026. It became Shakira's highest placement on the chart since she reached number five in 2007 with "Beautiful Liar" with Beyoncé and Burna Boy's first appearance on the chart in his career.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-27)
In Germany, the song peaked at number one on the [GfK Entertainment charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GfK_Entertainment_charts), becoming Shakira's fifth song to reach the top spot.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-28) On 6 August 2026, the song was named as the "Song of the Summer" by the [GfK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GfK), for topping the official chart for over five weeks.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-29)
Live performances
[
[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dai_Dai&action=edit§ion=6)]
On 11 June 2026, Shakira and Burna Boy performed the song live during the [opening ceremony of the World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_FIFA_World_Cup_opening_ceremonies) in [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City).[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-30) The song was then added to the setlist of the [Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Mujeres_Ya_No_Lloran_World_Tour), during the second US leg.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-31) Shakira and Burna Boy performed the song again on 19 July 2026, at the [2026 FIFA World Cup final halftime show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_FIFA_World_Cup_final_halftime_show) in [East Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Rutherford,_New_Jersey), [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey), outside [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City), with the [Ghetto Kids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghetto_Kids) as backup dancers.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-32)
Music video
[
[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dai_Dai&action=edit§ion=7)]
The music video for the song, directed by [Hannah Lux Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannah_Lux_Davis), was filmed in [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida), and released on 23 May 2026, on the singers' YouTube channel.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-33) The music video opens with cameos by footballers including [Lionel Messi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Messi), [Kylian Mbappé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kylian_Mbappé), and [Erling Haaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erling_Haaland). The video also features an animated reconstruction of Shakira standing over [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City)'s [Angel of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_of_Independence), and ends with a view of a graphically designed [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan) skyline including the [Empire State Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_State_Building).[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-34)
Throughout the video, Shakira performs choreographed dance routines with groups of dancers, while Burna Boy appears in separate performance scenes. The choreography incorporates Shakira's established dance styles, including fluid hip movements, body isolations, and Latin pop choreography, alongside movements influenced by African dance traditions that complement Burna Boy's musical style. Large [ensemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_ensemble) dance sequences and stadium-inspired formations reinforce the video's celebration of football and international unity.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-35)
On September 6, 2026, the music video reached 1 billion views on YouTube, becoming the first music video released in 2026 to do so.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-36)

https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-be.content:
Trending on Billboard
 [Shakira](https://www.billboard.com/artist/shakira/) and [Burna Boy](https://www.billboard.com/artist/burna-boy/)’s “Dai Dai (FIFA World Cup Official Song 2026)” nets the top spot on the [Billboard Global Excl. U.S.](https://www.billboard.com/charts/billboard-global-excl-us) chart. The song is the first official World Cup anthem to reach a No. 1 goal on the ranking, which began in 2020, after one other such song hit the top 10: Jung Kook’s No. 4-peaking “Dreamers (Music From the FIFA World Cup Qatar 2022).”
 Meanwhile, [Olivia Rodrigo](https://www.billboard.com/artist/olivia-rodrigo/)’s “Stupid Song” holds at No. 1 in its second week on the [Billboard Global 200](https://www.billboard.com/charts/billboard-global-200).
Shooting 7-1, “Dai Dai” dominates in its sixth week on Global Excl. U.S. with 31.5 million streams (up 6% week over week) and 4,000 sold (down 36%) outside the United States June 19-25, according to Luminate.
Shakira earns her second Global Excl. U.S. No. 1, after “TQG,” with Karol G, led in its debut week in March 2023. Burna Boy rules the ranking for the first time. Three acts from Colombia have led the list: Shakira, Karol G and Maluma, via “Hawái,” with The Weeknd (for one week in 2020). Before Burna Boy, one artist from Nigeria was No. 1: Rema, with “Calm Down,” with Selena Gomez (two weeks, 2023).
 Shakira and Burna Boy [performed](https://www.billboard.com/lists/world-cup-opening-ceremony-shakira-dai-dai-best-moments/) “Dai Dai” for a reported 80,000-plus fans at the FIFA World Cup 2026 opening ceremony June 11 at Mexico City’s Estadio Azteca. Soccer’s seminal tournament runs through July 19 — when Shakira, BTS and Madonna are set to take the stage at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J., for the first-ever World Cup final [halftime show](https://www.billboard.com/music/music-news/world-cup-halftime-bts-madonna-shakira-1236247959/).
BTS’ “Swim” keeps at No. 2 after eight weeks atop Global Excl. U.S. since April; Ariana Grande’s “Hate That I Made You Love Me” is steady at No. 3 after spending its first two weeks on the chart at No. 1 earlier in June; Michael Jackson’s “Billie Jean” jumps 8-4 after reaching No. 2; and “Stupid Song” falls to No. 5 a week after it launched at the summit.
“Stupid Song” leads the Global 200 with 45.9 million streams (down 32%) and 2,000 sold (down 46%) worldwide.
“Hate That I Made You Love Me” rebounds 3-2 after it topped the Global 200 in its debut week; “Billie Jean” bumps 6-3 following a week at No. 1 in May; and Rodrigo rounds out the top five with “The Cure,” down to No. 5 from its No. 2 high, and “Drop Dead,” which dips 4-5 after it led in its debut week in May.
Plus, “Dai Dai” surges 20-9 on the Global 200, led by 35.2 million streams (up 5%) in the U.S. It’s Shakira’s third top 10 on the chart and Burna Boy’s first.
The Billboard Global 200 and Global Excl. U.S. charts rank songs based on streaming and sales activity culled from more than 200 territories around the world, as compiled by Luminate. The Global 200 is inclusive of worldwide data and the Global Excl. U.S. chart comprises data from territories excluding the United States.
Chart ranks are based on a weighted formula incorporating official-only streams on both subscription and ad-supported tiers of audio and video music services, as well as download sales, the latter of which reflect purchases from full-service digital music retailers from around the world, with sales from direct-to-consumer (D2C) sites excluded from the charts’ calculations.
The latest charts, dated July 4, 2026, will update on Billboard.com tomorrow, June 30. For both tallies, the top 100 titles are available to all readers on Billboard.com, while the complete 200-title rankings are visible on Billboard Pro, Billboard’s subscription-based service. For all chart news, you can follow @billboard and @billboardcharts on both X, formerly known as Twitter, and Instagram.
Luminate, the independent data provider to the Billboard charts, completes a thorough review of all data submissions used in compiling the weekly chart rankings. Luminate reviews and authenticates data. In partnership with Billboard, data deemed suspicious or unverifiable is removed, using established criteria, before final chart calculations are made and published.

Marine Le Pen à Liévin (Pas-de-Calais), le 4 juillet 2026.
Tom Nicholson / REUTERS
RÉCIT - La chef de file du RN, condamnée à 1 an de prison ferme aménageable, sera candidate pour la quatrième fois à l’élection présidentielle. Elle a décidé de se pourvoir en cassation.
Marine Le Pen, 57 ans, est toujours la « candidate naturelle » du Rassemblement national (RN), après un coup théâtre extraordinaire comme la politique française en a le secret. Mardi soir, invitée du « 20 Heures » de TF1, la députée nationaliste du Pas-de-Calais a annoncé qu’elle se lançait dans sa quatrième campagne présidentielle. Néanmoins, au même moment, elle a annoncé qu’elle allait se pourvoir en cassation après sa condamnation, persuadée que ce nouveau rendez-vous judiciaire n’aura aucune conséquence sur sa candidature. Une situation complètement inédite dans l’histoire de la Ve République.
Une chose est certaine : l’arrêt de la cour d’appel de Paris n’a pas mis fin au rêve de la championne populiste et nationaliste de conquérir le pouvoir. Les juges ont finalement pris au mot Marine Le Pen après l’avoir condamnée à 3 ans de prison, dont 2 avec sursis, et à 45 mois d’inéligibilité, dont 30 avec sursis. Concrètement, la chef de file du RN devra purger un an de prison…

REPORTAGE - Déplacements écourtés, prises de parole reportées… Le candidat d’Horizons, qui a axé cette semaine sa campagne sur la retraite à 65 ans et la lutte contre le narcotrafic, fait face à la difficulté de tenir un agenda mis à mal par les crises.
ENTRETIEN - Dans son dernier essai iconoclaste, l’investisseur basé à Hongkong tente de donner un sens aux décisions économiques et géopolitiques de Donald Trump et Xi Jinping. Il tire des leçons, chinoises notamment, pour l’Europe et la France.

Propos acerbes du candidat d’Horizons dans un livre, critiques du chef de Renaissance contre ceux qui «cherchent à endormir cette campagne»… Les deux ex-premiers ministres ne se ménagent pas, malgré leur appel à l’apaisement pour viser l’union d’ici au premier tour de la présidentielle.

https://www.lefigaro.fr/politique/preser.content:
Marine Le Pen à La Flèche (Sarthe) le 8 juillet 2026, au lendemain de sa condamnation par la cour d’appel de Paris.
Benoit Tessier / REUTERS
DÉCRYPTAGE - La cour d’appel de Paris a justifié la réduction de la peine d’inéligibilité de Marine Le Pen par un motif inspiré d’une décision du Conseil constitutionnel, qui nuance la sévérité des lois visant les responsables politiques coupables d’atteintes à la probité.
L’argumentation est développée à la page 302 de l’arrêt rendu mardi par la cour d’appel de Paris dans l’affaire des assistants parlementaires européens de l’ancien Front national. Les magistrats ont confirmé la condamnation de Marine Le Pen pour détournement de fonds publics, mais ont réduit sa peine d’inéligibilité. De cinq ans en première instance, celle-ci est passée à 45 mois, dont 15 mois ferme. Sachant que le tribunal avait ordonné l’exécution provisoire (c’est-à-dire immédiate) de cette peine en première instance, en mars 2025, Marine Le Pen a purgé cette peine et peut donc légalement se présenter à l’élection présidentielle. Ce qu’elle a annoncé lundi sur TF1, tout en formant un pourvoi en cassation pour éviter de porter un bracelet électronique.
Pourquoi cette volte-face de la justice qui, en appel, a soigneusement calculé une durée d’inéligibilité permettant à Marine Le Pen de concourir en 2027 ? Selon son arrêt, «la cour juge en effet que l’exécution de la peine complémentaire…

Plusieurs responsables politiques du centre, de la droite et du Rassemblement national ont assisté samedi à la messe célébrée par le pape Léon XIV place de la Concorde. Les principales figures de gauche étaient, elles, absentes, plusieurs ayant choisi de participer aux marches pour le climat.
«Qu’une génération ne pense pas à la génération suivante, qu’elle lui impose, sans le lui dire, la charge d’avoir à payer pendant des décennies, des facilités que nous avons rencontrées aujourd’hui, ce n’est pas normal», s’est agacé le chef du gouvernement ce jeudi.
RÉCIT - Mediapart prétend avoir publié les « preuves » que le président du RN a bien tenu des propos antisémites en 2013. Le parti balaie les accusations, mais la campagne nationaliste pourrait vaciller.
DÉCRYPTAGE - Marine Le Pen et Jordan Bardella doivent présenter le contre-budget nationaliste la semaine prochaine, et se projeter sur les cinq premières années du quinquennat, si jamais la candidate RN arrivait à conquérir l’Élysée.
ANALYSE - Promettant un effort de 54 milliards d’euros l’année prochaine, le premier ministre doit détailler sa copie jeudi. Et trouver les moyens d’éviter la censure grâce au PS ou au RN.
EXCLUSIF - À moins de sept mois du premier tour, les candidats du RN et d’Horizons semblent en capacité de se qualifier pour la finale, selon notre baromètre Ifop-Fiducial pour Le Figaro, LCI et Sud Radio.
RÉCIT - Alors que la candidate RN a redit sa « confiance absolue » envers son héritier politique, qui continue de démentir les propos antisémites qui lui sont attribués par Mediapart, le duo nationaliste dénonce les « prémices d’une guerre totale ».
REPORTAGE - La sœur aînée de Marine Le Pen est tête de liste dans ce département devenu un laboratoire du parti nationaliste. Elle entend profiter de l’« effondrement de la droite » pour y être élue.
CHRONIQUE - À mesure que la présidentielle approche, le désir de changement profond gagne toutes les familles politiques. Les Français veulent rompre avec l’existant sans se jeter dans l’inconnu.
RÉCIT - Alors que plusieurs polémiques ont marqué le début de campagne de Marine Le Pen, les élus du RN ferment de plus en plus les écoutilles avec la presse, regrettant que des « taupes » alimentent depuis quelques semaines certains journalistes.
RÉCIT - Seul candidat à la tête du parti à la flamme, le patron du Rassemblement national se prépare à être reconduit à la faveur d’un congrès prévu fin octobre.

During the appeal trial, Le Pen denied that the National Rally had a system to embezzle European Parliament funds and said the party acted in "good faith."
France's far-right chief Marine Le Pen said she still intended to run for president in 2027 despite a Paris appeals court handing her one year of house arrest over a fake jobs scam in the European parliament.
"Tonight, I am a candidate in the presidential election," Le Pen told TF1 television on Tuesday evening.
Earlier on Tuesday, the appeals court handed Le pen, who has run for president three times before, a 45-month ban from office, 30 months of which were suspended.
The other 15 months were expected to be backdated from the initial verdict by a lower court in March last year and therefore to have expired, meaning she could in theory be a candidate.
But the court also gave her a three-year detention, two of which were suspended, meaning she must serve one year under house arrest wearing an electronic ankle tag.
The three-time presidential candidate has said she would not compete to replace centrist President Emmanuel Macron if she was under house arrest and could not campaign properly.
"When you're a presidential candidate, you need to be completely free to move around," she said last week in a televised interview.
"I can't depend on a magistrate to allow me to go to a rally."
'Witch hunt'
The first trial last year found Le Pen, along with 24 former European lawmakers, assistants and accountants, as well as the anti-immigration party itself, guilty of operating a system from 2004-2016 to use European Parliament funds to employ RN staff in France.
The court sentenced Le Pen to a five-year ban from public office and four years in prison, with two suspended.
Le Pen claimed her party was the victim of a "witch hunt" and some supporters sent the judges death threats. Le Pen, the party and 10 others appealed.
During the appeal trial, she denied that the RN had a system to embezzle European Parliament funds and has said her party acted in "complete good faith."
But prosecutors alleged she "professionalised" a way to divert EU funds first introduced haphazardly by her late father, party co-founder Jean-Marie Le Pen, after she took over its leadership from him in 2011.
Recent opinion polls have largely suggested the far right will lead in the first round of next year's vote, but are divided on the outcome of the second round.
Opinion polls
Many have shown slightly better results for National Rally president Jordan Bardella than his colleague Le Pen, but their adversaries have inferred the veteran politician would be a fiercer opponent.
"This woman is very intelligent, she's not here by chance. And if she does also run for a fourth time, she won't be an opponent we can sneer at," hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has said.
An opinion poll in May suggested Le Pen could win the runoffs next year if she is allowed to compete.
The Harris Interactive Toluna survey of more than 1,700 registered voters projected her winning, against Melenchon as well as centrist former prime ministers Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe.
Other polls have, however, suggested Philippe, who is also courting right-wing voters, could win a runoff against the far right.

https://www.politico.eu/article/marine-l.content:
Le Pen verdict: Surprise ruling complicates French far right’s presidential plans
An appeals court ruling technically allows the French far-right leader to run in next year’s election, but she’d have to campaign while under house arrest.
PARIS — An appeals court on Tuesday cleared a possible path for Marine Le Pen to stand in next year’s presidential election — but under conditions she previously said she would not accept.
The three-judge panel that heard the far-right leader’s appeal upheld her conviction for embezzling European Parliament funds but, crucially, tossed her immediate five-year ban on running for office and replaced it with a shorter one that, technically, allows her to run.
However, Le Pen was sentenced to a year of house arrest, and as recently as last week she said she would not run for president while wearing an ankle bracelet.
Advertisement
“If the idea is to allow me to run for office but prevent me from campaigning freely, that won’t work,” Le Pen said in an interview on Wednesday. “I believe that when you’re a presidential candidate, you need to have complete freedom of movement. That’s not the case if you’re wearing an electronic ankle monitor.”
The conditions of Le Pen’s house arrest, which could allow her to travel for work, will be determined at a later date by a separate judge.
The decision was unexpected and appeared to confuse Le Pen and others from her party, the National Rally, who were in court when the ruling was delivered.
Presiding Judge Michèle Agi did not explain why Le Pen’s ineligibility period had been reduced. But Agi said the court concluded that the defendants had swindled European taxpayers out of an estimated €2.8 million by hiring assistants who spent most of their time on domestic party politics rather than their official European Parliament duties. Agi added Le Pen bore significant responsibility as a party leader.
Le Pen is expected to address her future during a primetime interview at 8 p.m. She did not speak after leaving the Palais de Justice in central Paris, but her lawyer called the court’s decision “a good start.”
After court, Le Pen and some of her closest lieutenants headed to their party headquarters to meet with Jordan Bardella, her 30-year-old protégé and potential replacement as presidential candidate.
Advertisement
Should Le Pen stand down, it would be a massive personal blow. She has already run for president three times, but polls show the National Rally has never had a better chance of winning the presidency than it does next year.
Opinion polls indicate that Bardella is slightly more popular than Le Pen, but his age and limited experience have sparked concerns among party insiders about whether he can withstand the rigors of a presidential campaign or is ready to take the reins of one of the most powerful offices in the world.
The French presidency concentrates sweeping executive authority in the hands of a leader who oversees the globe’s seventh-largest economy, commands a nuclear-armed state and holds a permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council.
But there are differences in how Le Pen and Bardella would govern the country.
Le Pen’s catch-all brand of economic policies, which includes the defense of much of the French welfare state, has long been met with disdain by conservative and business circles which deemed it unserious.
Bardella, on the other hand, has tried extending his party’s appeal to a broader right-wing electorate by striking a more pro-market tone.

A. Introduction
1. This report of the Director General is on the implementation of the NPT Safeguards Agreement 1,2 in
the Islamic Republic of Iran (Iran). It covers the pe riod since the issuance of the Director General’s
previous quarterly report.3
B. Safeguards implementation
2. The Director General, on 13 June 2025, reported to the Board of Governors (Board) and to the
United Nations Security Council (Security Council) th at the Agency had been informed of a military
operation launched by Israel, which included attacks on several of Iran’s nuclear facilities. 4 These attacks
took place between 13-24 June 2025. Consequently, the Agency stoppe d conducting verification activities

by Iran on 18 December 2003. Iran implemented voluntarily the Additional Protocol between December 2003 and February
2006. On 16 January 2016, Iran began provisionally applying the A dditional Protocol in accordance with Article 17(b) of the

in Iran. By the end of June 2025, the Agency had d ecided to withdraw all of its inspectors from Iran for
safety reasons. On 2 July 2025, Iran enacted a law suspending cooperation with the Agency. 5 Since
13 June 2025, the Agency has not received nuclear material accountancy reports and updated design
information questionnaires (DIQs), and has not had access to any safeguarded nuclear facilities in Iran,
with the exception of the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant (BNPP). The Agency, through the analysis of
commercially available satellite imagery and open sources, continues to monitor developments at Iran’s
nuclear facilities.
Chronology
3. The Director General, in his statement to the Board of Governors on 13 June 2025, recalled the
relevant General Conference resolutions on the subject of military attacks against nuclear facilities, which
provided, inter alia, that “any armed attack on and threat against nuclear facilities devoted to peaceful
purposes constitutes a violation of the principles of th e United Nations Charter, international law and the
Statute of the Agency”.6 The Director General also reiterated that he had repeatedly stated that nuclear
facilities must never be attacked, regardless of the cont ext or circumstances, as it could harm both people
and the environment, and that such attacks have serious implications for nuclear safety, security and
safeguards, as well as regional and international peace and security.
4. Following the commencement of the military attacks on several of Iran’s nuclear facilities, the
Agency stopped all in-field verification and monitori ng activities in Iran for safety reasons, to which Iran
agreed.
5. The military attacks, in which the United States of America also later participated, lasted until
24 June 2025. During this period the Director Genera l provided updates on the status of Iran’s nuclear
and nuclear-related facilities, based on the Agency’s assessments of commercially available satellite
imagery, to the Board and the Security Council (see GOV/2025/50 for details).
6. The facilities known to have contained nuclear mate rial affected by the military attacks were: the
Fordow Fuel Enrichment Plant (FFEP); the Fuel Enrich ment Plant (FEP); the Pilot Fuel Enrichment Plant
(PFEP); the Uranium Conversion Facility (UCF); the Fuel Manufacturing Plant (FMP); the Fuel Plate
Fabrication Plant (FPFP); and the Enriched UO 2 Powder Plant (EUPP). In addition, the Khondab Heavy
Water Research Reactor (KHRR), which was under construction a nd did not contain nuclear material,
was also affected.
7. In a letter to the Director General dated 13 June 202 5, the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Iran, HE
Mr Abbas Araghchi, indicated that Iran would “adopt special measures to protect our nuclear equipment
and materials”. The Director General, in his letter of reply of the same day, indicated that any transfers of
nuclear material from a safeguarded facility to another location in Iran must be declared to the Agency,
as required under Iran’s NPT Safeguards Agreement, a nd expressed his readiness to work with Iran on
the matter.
8. As noted above, by the end of June 2025, taking into account safety considerations arising from the
military attacks, the Agency had decided to withdraw all of its inspectors from Iran.
9. On 2 July 2025, President Masoud Pezeshkian re portedly signed a law adopted by the Parliament
of Iran to suspend cooperation with the Agency. According to this law, such cooperation must be

have been met.
10. The Director General, in a letter to Foreign Mini ster Abbas Araghchi dated 12 July 2025, indicated
that it was important to re-establish normal collaborati on between Iran and the Agency in order to ensure
compliance with the NPT Safeguards Agreement. He also indicated that in view of the possible impact
on the implementation of safeguards in Iran deriving from the recently adopted Iranian domestic law it
was essential and urgent to arrive at an agreement on the modalities that could guarantee the necessary
compliance. To that effect, he indicated his willingness to meet in Vienna or elsewhere.
11. Following discussions between the Director General and Iran’s Permanent Representative to the
IAEA, Ambassador Reza Najafi, on 23 July 2025, Iran agr eed to a technical team from the Agency visiting
Iran for high-level consultations on “temporary practical arrangements” to address Iran’s concerns and to
enable the resumption of Agency verification activities.
12. The Agency, in a letter dated 30 July 2025, reminded Iran that the Agency’s timeliness7 for the
detection of the diversion of one significant quantity (SQ) of high enriched uranium (HEU) is one month 8
and, therefore, verification of Iran’s declared inventory of HEU was overdue.
13. On 11 August 2025, a technical team from the Ag ency held discussions in Tehran with senior
Iranian officials on “temporary practical arrangements” to address Iran’s concerns and to enable the
resumption of Agency verification activities. Iran referred to the need for “separate arrangements”
between Iran and the Agency relating to how they intend to proceed in their future dealings with one
another, including procedures for conducting verification activities. The Agency, while taking into
account concerns expressed by Iran, emphasized that a ny new arrangement should be implemented in the
framework of the NPT Safeguards Agreement.
14. Iran, in a letter dated 14 August 2025, provided a detailed draft of “a new Arrangement”. This
included a number of elements beyond the Agency’s verification responsibilities under the NPT
Safeguards Agreement and its Subsidiary Arrangements. In relation to the resumption of Agency
verification activities, Iran proposed that, for undama ged facilities, the Agency “shall submit its requests
[for inspection] on a case by case basis” and, with rega rd to damaged facilities, Iran undertook to provide
the Agency with a report “up to one month after the finalization of this Arrangement”. Following the
submission of such a report, Iran and the Agency would “negotiate and agree on the arrangements for
cooperation”.
15. The Director General, in his reply dated 15 Augus t 2025, made clear that it was indispensable and
urgent to restart safeguards activities in Iran in acco rdance with the NPT Safeguards Agreement and that
implementation of the Agreement cannot be suspended under any circumstances. He also presented a
number of concrete steps, including the preparation by Iran of special reports for HEU and low enriched
uranium (LEU) for the affected facilities and updated DIQs. 9 The Director General also expressed the
Agency’s readiness to discuss with Iran the modalities for accessing those facilities and conducting
inspections and DIVs. For facilities unaffected by the military attacks, the Agency would continue to
provide advance notice for inspections and DIVs.

facility (see GOV/2014/41, Section C.4).7 The longer the Agency is unable to verify the inventories of declared nuclear material
in Iran, therefore, the greater the risk that the Agency is unable to provide such assurance.

16. In the same letter, the Agency indicated its readiness to discu ss updated safeguards approaches for
facilities under safeguards in Iran to take into account Iran’s security concerns, provided that such
approaches remain consistent with the rights and obligations of Iran and the Agency under the NPT
Safeguards Agreement.
17. On 19 August 2025, the Agency provided advance notice to Iran for inspections and DIVs to be
carried out by the Agency at three unaffected nuclear facilities.
18. On 22 August 2025, a technical team from the Agency held further discussions with senior Iranian
officials in Vienna on practical steps on safeguards implementation in Iran pursuant to the NPT
Safeguards Agreement following the military attacks on its safeguarded nuclear facilities. No agreement
was reached on such practical steps, and the Agency and Iran decided to continue the discussions.
19. On 27 and 28 August 2025, the Agency conducted two inspections at the BNPP as part of its routine

20. As of the date of issuance of this report, furthe r discussions between the Agency and senior Iranian
officials on practical steps relating to safeguards implementation in Iran pursuant to the NPT Safeguards
Agreement are planned to take place in Vienna in the next few days.
C. Unresolved safeguards issues
C.1. Comprehensive Assessment
21. The Director General’s previous quarterly report, 10 in response to the Board’s request contained in
resolution GOV/2024/68, provided a “comprehensive and updated assessment on the possible presence
or use of undeclared nuclear material in connection with past and present outstanding issues regarding
Iran’s nuclear programme”. The report identified a num ber of unresolved safeguard s issues related, inter
alia, to Iran not declaring nuclear material and nuclear-related activities at undeclared locations; the
possible presence of undeclared nuclear material in Iran; and the limited cooperation from Iran.
C.2. Board Resolution
22. The Board considered the Director General’s report and, on 12 June 2025, adopted resolution
GOV/2025/38 in which the Board, inter alia:
  found that “Iran’s many failures to uphold its obligations… constitutes non-compliance with
 its obligations under its Safeguards Ag reement” (operative paragraph 3);
  found that “the Agency is not able to verify that there has been no diversion of nuclear
 material” (operative paragraph 4);
  reaffirmed its decision that “it is essential and urgent in order to ensure verification of the non-
 diversion of nuclear material that Iran act to fulf il its legal obligations” (operative paragraph 7);
  called upon Iran to “urgently remedy its non-compliance with its Safeguards Agreement”
 (operative paragraph 10); and
  decided to remain seized of the matter (operative paragraph 13).

C.3. Recent developments
23. There has been no engagement between Iran and the Agency on the unresolved safeguards issues
described in the Director General’s previous report (GOV/2025/25) during this reporting period.
D. Other issues
24. Following an inspection at FFEP on 14 May 2025, the Ag ency inspectors at the end of the inspection
kept some pages of the DIQ that were used during th e inspection and brought them to Vienna instead of
returning them to the Agency’s working place at the facility. It should be stressed that while these pages
contained some description of the interior of the faci lity, they did not include content that compromised
the security of the facility. In a letter to Iran date d 27 May 2025, the Agency informed Iran that as soon
as the oversight – which the Agency regretted – was noti ced, the pages were returned to the State authority
at the earliest opportunity – on 26 May 2025. Iran, in a letter dated 14 August 2025, indicated that the
actions of the two inspectors involved “constitute a breach of certain provisions under the Comprehensive
Safeguards Agreement” and objected to “the continued designation of the two inspectors”. The Agency
considers Iran’s decision to withdraw the designation of these two experienced inspectors as unjustified
because the incident did not involve any breach of confidentiality.
E. Summary
25. The withdrawal of all Agency inspectors from Iran because of safety concerns arising from the
military attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities was necessary given the overall security situation. Iran’s
subsequent decision to suspend cooperation with the Agency is deeply regrettable. Despite this
development, the Agency has repeatedly reached out to Iran. The Director General, in letters to Iran’s
Foreign Minister, has reiterated his own and the Agen cy’s disposition to take into consideration Iran’s
security concerns, bearing in mind the law adopted by Iran.
26. While acknowledging the need to agree on technical , practical steps to enable the resumption of
safeguards implementation, it must be recalled that Iran’s inventory of HEU, the only NPT non-nuclear-
weapon State to have produced such nuclear material, is a matter of serious concern which must be
addressed. The Agency has not had access to verify this specific nuclear material in Iran for over two and
a half months, which means that its verification – according to Agency standard safeguards practice – is
overdue.
27. Without the full implementation of safeguards in Iran being resumed, the Agency will not be in a
position to provide any conclusion or assuran ce regarding Iran’s nuclear programme.
28. In that context, technical modalities to enable the full resumption of Agency inspections should be
concluded without delay. The Director General expresses his conviction that agreement on such
modalities is possible.
29. The Director General will continue to report as appropriate.

# IAEA Director General's Introductory Statement to the Board of Governors

[![](/sites/default/files/2026-09/dg-bog-september-approved-photo.jpg)](http://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/2026-09/dg-bog-september-approved-photo.jpg)

IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi delivers his statement at the opening of the Board of Governors meeting held at the Agency headquarters in Vienna, Austria, 7 September 2026. (Photo: D. Calma/IAEA)

*(As prepared for delivery)*

Ladies and gentlemen,

In a fragmented world, the IAEA is more indispensable than ever. Our impartial and expert work is part of some of the most sensitive and consequential international efforts of our time.

Over the past three months, we have been part of progress that has strengthened the foundations of peace and security, and we have also been working amid tensions and conflict that are raising the risks of a nuclear accident.

First, let me mention the historic breakthrough in safeguards implementation matters that has occurred in the Syrian Arab Republic.

Last month, I stood at Dair Alzour, a site where the IAEA assessed previously that a building destroyed in 2007 was very likely a nuclear reactor under construction that Syria was required to declare to the Agency under its NPT Safeguards Agreement. Syria’s new government agreed to provide information and grant the IAEA access to the Dair Alzour site and other locations in Syria to address the outstanding safeguards issues stemming from the country’s past nuclear activities.

Having received the necessary access and information from Syria, and based on the evaluation of the safeguards-relevant information available to it, the Agency has been able to clarify and resolve the Agency’s questions concerning the outstanding safeguards issues related to Syria’s past nuclear activities.

I welcome Syria’s transparency and cooperation with the Agency which facilitates the resolution of the outstanding safeguards issues related to Syria’s past nuclear activities. I will provide more details of this progress a little later in my statement.

Next, I need to inform you of the delicate nuclear safety situation at Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP).

A reliable supply of electricity is essential to powering the ZNPP’s safety and security functions, most notably the pumps that cool all six reactors and their spent fuel pools.

Since June alone, the ZNPP has experienced 10 losses of off-site power, bringing the total since the start of the conflict to 26.

The frequent interruptions to the plant’s two power lines, leading to its reliance on emergency diesel generators, pose serious risks. They violate both the Seven Indispensable Pillars for ensuring nuclear safety and security during an armed conflict and the Five Concrete Principles for protecting the ZNPP.

Since 20 August, the ZNPP’s emergency diesel generators have been supplying power at the plant after military activity on the northern side of the Dnipro River severed the connection to the 330 kilovolt (kV) Ferosplavna-1 line.

As the ZNPP’s emergency generators drained the available diesel to little more than a week of supplies, forcing its cooling pumps to be run only intermittently, I continued my persistent efforts to broker a ceasefire so that the Ferosplavna-1 power line could be repaired.

The seventh ceasefire took hold this weekend, allowing demining and repair work to begin.

Both sides have engaged constructively with the IAEA to help make this localized ceasefire possible, showing that practical steps can be taken, even in extremely difficult circumstances, to improve nuclear safety.

IAEA teams on the ground are monitoring the demining and repair work, which are expected to conclude shortly.

Though repairs to the plant’s second line — the 750 kV Dniprovska power line — were completed in June under the sixth ceasefire arrangement negotiated by the Agency, the line remains unavailable because of severe damage at the associated Dniprovska substation.

It goes without saying that nuclear power plant staff must be able to carry out their essential work without being attacked or placed at risk. I solemnly call on all military commanders in the region to stop attacks on nuclear power plants and their staff, and to exercise maximum military restraint.

I say this, because last month a drone explosion at a bus stop used by plant staff and subcontractors travelling to Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Plant caused multiple casualties. The ZNPP informed the IAEA team at the plant that the explosion caused 20 casualties, including one death and three serious injuries.

The loss of life is a tragedy.

Endangering personnel is a clear violation of the IAEA’s Seven Indispensable Pillars for ensuring nuclear safety and security during armed conflict.

The security situation around the plant also remains a serious concern. Our teams continue to report frequent military activity in the vicinity of the site and of Enerhodar, including incidents affecting critical infrastructure and plant personnel.

Across Ukraine, threats to nuclear safety and security persist, with our teams continuing to report military activity in their monitoring areas.

During its latest mission, conducted between late July and early August, the Agency visited 13 substations essential for maintaining nuclear safety and security. The mission confirmed continued damage to grid infrastructure and limited restoration progress.

Military activity near nuclear power plants and on the electricity grid continues to pose risks that must be avoided. I renew my call for maximum military restraint from all sides.

The Agency's presence on the ground remains as important as ever. Since the beginning of our continuous presence in Ukraine, 185 Agency staff members have participated in 287 missions, representing a total of 645 person-months of work to help reduce the risk of a nuclear accident.

Through the IAEA Support and Assistance Mission to the Kherson Oblast, nine Ukrainian professionals were trained at Seibersdorf in non-destructive testing for post-disaster structural assessments.

The Agency's assistance programme continues to provide indispensable support where it is needed most. More than 250 deliveries of equipment have now been provided to Ukraine, with a total value exceeding €27 million. They include nuclear safety and security equipment, power supply systems, radiation monitoring instruments, physical protection equipment and medical assistance. Additional support has continued through our dedicated programmes addressing the consequences of the Kakhovka dam destruction and the safety and security of radioactive sources.

Sustaining these efforts will require continued support from Member States. Current unfunded priority needs amount to approximately €17 million. I encourage those in a position to do so to continue supporting the Agency's efforts in preventing a nuclear accident from adding to the suffering during this conflict.

Ukraine is not the only place where nuclear facilities have been threatened by conflict. The IAEA’s Incident and Emergency Centre (IEC) in Vienna operates 24/7, closely monitoring all developments, including those in the Gulf region, where we maintain continual contact with the competent authorities. Based on data reported to the IAEA, radiation levels in the region remain at normal background levels.

Let me repeat what I have said before: nuclear safety is fundamental and applicable to all, without exception. An attack on any facility, wherever in the world it is located, creates unacceptable risks to people and the environment in which they live.

Mr Chairperson,

Here in Vienna, we are preparing for the 70th regular session of the General Conference, which is taking place 14–18 September. The interest from Member States has been very high, in terms of the number of delegations, their size and their level of seniority.

At the Treaty Event, taking place on Wednesday, 16 September, I will again welcome Member States to deposit with me instruments of adherence in relation to treaties for which I serve as depositary. The event highlights the concrete steps taken by Member States to strengthen the international legal framework for the safe, secure and peaceful uses of nuclear technology. I encourage Member States to participate, and I look forward to recognizing their commitment to our shared objectives.

The Scientific Forum, taking place 15–16 September, has the theme: *Rays of Hope: Delivering on the Promise of Cancer Care*. The cancer crisis continues to burden patients, their families and communities and the healthcare systems of many of our Member States. But it does not have to be this way. Real action to expand equitable access to life-saving cancer care is making a difference.

Since I launched Rays of Hope in 2022, the IAEA has been working with Member States and a growing network of partners, including international financial institutions, international organizations, the private sector and other stakeholders to turn commitments into concrete progress. The Rays of Hope Anchor Centre network has grown to twenty centres and now functions as a truly collaborative system of regional support.

The upcoming Scientific Forum is an important opportunity to take stock of what we have achieved together, reflect on the partnerships that have made this progress possible, and find ways to build on this momentum to reach even more people with the cancer care they need.

Getting radiation doses right in medicine is essential. In October, the Agency will host the *International Symposium on Standards, Applications and Quality Assurance in Medical Radiation Dosimetry*, bringing together experts from medical institutions, research centres and standards laboratories.

Experts from 20 Member States have met to advance the production and quality control of Actinium-225 radiopharmaceuticals, establishing new collaboration with industry to address the supply bottlenecks limiting access to targeted alpha therapy, an advanced cancer treatment that destroys cancer cells while sparing healthy tissue.

The first 18 students have graduated from the Master's Programme in Nutrition and Nuclear Techniques, 16 of them at the International University of Rabat in Morocco and 2 at North-West University in South Africa. They return to their countries equipped to strengthen national nutrition programmes.

Global interest in Atoms4Food continues to grow, with 46 Member States now participating. Assessment missions have been completed in 6 countries, most recently in Liberia in July, each identifying country-specific needs and shaping a national action plan. New contributions from Australia, the United States and private partners are advancing work on soil and water management, crop improvement, human nutrition and animal health.

Cross-border tsetse fly control activities were launched in Senegal and the Gambia, building on earlier suppression campaigns in the Niayes region. A new coordinated research project on the New World Screwworm will bring together experts from more than 20 affected countries to advance surveillance and sustainable pest control. New projects were also launched on seafood authenticity, involving 23 Member States, and on soil contamination involving — so called “forever chemicals” (PFAS). Demand for food irradiation continues to grow, with Israel, Brunei Darussalam, Mongolia, Rwanda and Jamaica seeking to adopt or expand its application.

Through ZODIAC, and in coordination with other international organizations, the Agency responded rapidly to the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Equipment and reagents for molecular and serological diagnostics have enabled the national ZODIAC laboratory to begin surveillance and response. The Agency also supported foot-and-mouth disease preparedness in Eswatini, African swine fever response in Nigeria and contagious bovine pleuropneumonia in Ghana, while strengthening preparedness for highly pathogenic avian influenza through the VETLAB Network and closer collaboration with the World Organization for Animal Health.

In July in Vienna, we launched the *NUTEC Plastics Marine Monitoring Network and its Common Database*, developed in house and in coordination with UNEP. This achieves, in five years and as planned, the objective set for the marine component of NUTEC Plastics. The 180 institutions from 110 Member States in the network now share a harmonized approach to microplastics monitoring, and a secure platform on which to store and exchange their data, generating comparable evidence to inform policy.

The GloWAL Network now comprises 71 participating laboratories. Its baseline survey, with responses from 145 counterparts in 70 Member States, identified priority needs in laboratory skills and data quality. With support from Australia, Slovenia, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the United States, the Network opened its first interlaboratory comparison exercise on isotopes in water in May. At the Isotope Hydrology Laboratory, all components for the custom-designed Atom Trap Trace Analysis instrument have been procured; once operational, it will enable krypton-81 analysis to assess the sustainability of deep, ancient groundwater reserves.

The Agency's transportable electron beam system has received regulatory approval and has been commissioned. It strengthens our capacity to deliver technical cooperation and on-site demonstrations worldwide.

Following the earthquake in Venezuela on 24 June, the Agency is providing specialized equipment, an expert mission and training so that national experts can safely assess damaged buildings and infrastructure.

Through Peaceful Uses Initiative projects supported by Japan, the Agency is helping Pacific Island Countries to measure radionuclides in their own waters and seafood. A review in June confirmed the readiness of the University of the South Pacific in Suva to host a regional hub.

The report on *Strengthening the Agency's Activities related to Nuclear Science, Technology and Applications*, now before the Board, provides an overview of the Agency’s work on nuclear power and non-power applications since the last General Conference.

Mr Chairperson,

The Agency's technical cooperation programme is currently supporting 152 Member States through more than 1000 projects, with the main areas of work in 2026 being health and nutrition, food and agriculture, and safety and security.

Preparations for the 2028–2029 technical cooperation cycle are well under way. So far, more than 480 concepts have been submitted for the new cycle, and of these, around 185 have moved on to the project design phase.

Contributions to the TC Fund, the main source of funding for the TC programme, are essential to ensure sufficient, assured and predictable resources. The TCF Rate of Attainment, as of mid-August, was 67 per cent, or €65.7 million. I thank Member States and ask that they pay their contributions on time and in full so that we can continue this indispensable work and fulfil our mandate.

Mr Chairperson,

The fifteenth *Symposium on International Safeguards* will take place here on 9–12 November, presenting an opportunity for State and regional authorities responsible for the implementation of safeguards, the research and development (R&D) community, industry, and civil society to identify challenges and opportunities for IAEA safeguards, to showcase research, to share ideas and to build partnerships.

As requested by the Board in its resolution GOV/2025/71 adopted in November last year, I have submitted to the Board a report on the *Implementation of the NPT Safeguards Agreement and relevant provisions of the United Nations Security Council resolutions in the Islamic Republic of Iran*.

As stated in the report, during this reporting period, the Agency has neither received information from Iran regarding the status of its declared nuclear material or facilities nor had access to any of those facilities to conduct in-field verification activities. Therefore, the Agency was unable to discharge its safeguards responsibilities under the NPT Safeguards Agreement at declared nuclear facilities in Iran.

Consequently, we were not able to verify their status for safeguards purposes and the associated nuclear material, and as a result I am also unable to report in relation to the implementation by Iran of relevant provisions of the UN Security Council resolutions or the Board’s resolutions of November last year and June this this year.

It is more than a year since the Agency lost continuity of knowledge in relation to the previously declared inventories of LEU and HEU enriched up to 60% U-235 at the declared nuclear facilities affected by the military attacks of June 2025.

The Agency’s lack of information about these facilities and associated nuclear material and our inability to conduct verification activities at these facilities is a matter of serious proliferation concern. The situation needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency.

I call on Iran to engage with the Agency constructively in order to make possible the full and effective implementation of Agency safeguards in Iran and to fulfill its responsibilities under the NPT Safeguards Agreement.

A return to diplomacy and negotiations aimed at finding a solution to issues related to Iran’s nuclear programme is imperative, and the Agency stands ready to support such efforts. The situation regarding Iran’s nuclear programme has implications on the global non-proliferation regime.

The number of States with safeguards agreements in force remains 193, and 146 of these States have additional protocols in force. I urge Equatorial Guinea, the only remaining non-nuclear-weapon State Party to the NPT without a comprehensive safeguards agreement in force, to bring this agreement into force without delay. I also reiterate my repeated calls for the remaining 11 States with small quantities protocols based on the original standard text to amend or rescind them as soon as possible. I encourage States that have not yet concluded additional protocols to do so as soon as possible.

The IAEA continues to monitor the nuclear programme of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

I have reported previously that the Agency is monitoring a new building at Yongbyon that has dimensions and infrastructure similar to the Kangson enrichment facility.  According to photographs taken in June this year, it appears to contain centrifuges of the same type as those depicted in previously released images of DPRK enrichment facilities.

The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of the DPRK’s production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern.

The Agency has observed indications that the 5MW(e) reactor at Yongbyon likely continues to operate in its seventh irradiation cycle.

The Agency has observed indications that, after a period of shutdown, the light water reactor (LWR) at Yongbyon has been operating since the end of April 2026.

The continuation and further development of the DPRK’s nuclear programme are clear violations of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and are deeply regrettable. The Agency continues to maintain its enhanced readiness to play its essential role in verifying the DPRK’s nuclear programme.

Mr Chairperson,

I have already mentioned the historical breakthrough in Syria. As you see from my report on the *Implementation of the NPT Safeguards Agreement in the Syrian Arab Republic*, the Syrian authorities have provided the necessary information and access and facilitated the Agency’s recent verification activities in Syria. This has served to bring previously undeclared nuclear material under Agency safeguards in accordance with Syria’s NPT Safeguards Agreement with the Agency and mutually agreed practical steps.

The nuclear material, along with the findings at the Dair Alzour site are consistent with the Agency’s previous assessment that a gas-cooled graphite‑moderated nuclear reactor was under construction at the Dair Alzour site in Syria under the previous Syrian government, which should have been declared to the Agency. Also, the design, quantities and characteristics of the fuel rods recently reported by Syria are consistent with the Agency’s previous assessment regarding the design and capacity of the nuclear reactor identified by the Agency.

On 27 August 2026, Syria provided the Agency with a design information questionnaire (DIQ) for the installation at the Dair Alzour site as a decommissioned reactor, as required under Syria’s NPT Safeguards Agreement.

As the excavation work continues at the Dair Alzour site, the Agency will continue to monitor activities.

As my report on the *Application of IAEA Safeguards in the Middle East* shows, there remain long-standing and fundamental differences of views among countries of the region regarding the application of comprehensive Agency safeguards to all nuclear activities. It has therefore not been possible to make further progress in fulfilling our mandate from the General Conference in this area. I will continue consultations.

With regard to nuclear-powered submarines, the Republic of Korea has formally notified the Secretariat of its intention to start consultations with the Agency on an arrangement pursuant to Article 14 of its comprehensive safeguards agreement (CSA) and reiterated its commitment to fulfill its obligations under the NPT, the CSA and the Additional Protocol. In this regard, the Republic of Korea has already provided the Secretariat with the relevant declarations. I look forward to the continuation of our consultations in the same spirit of transparency.

Mr Chairperson,

Detailed updates of our recent work in nuclear safety and security are found in two reports before the Board: The *Nuclear and Radiation Safety Report* and the *Nuclear Security Report 2026*.

In late June/early July, at the *International Conference on Topical Issues in Nuclear Installation Safety* participants highlighted the growing importance of international cooperation in emerging topics such as artificial intelligence, advanced reactors and maritime nuclear applications.

Ahead of next year’s second Conference of the Parties to the Amendment to the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material, the Meeting of the Preparatory Committee will take place from 30 September to 2 October, with Canada as chair.

In Japan, the Agency continues its independent review and monitoring of the discharge of ALPS-treated water from the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station. Japan has begun the discharge of the twenty-third batch of ALPS-treated water. Since operations began a total volume of more than 170 000 cubic metres has been discharged, the tritium concentrations of which have been far below Japan’s operational limit and consistent with international safety standards.

We continue to enhance the transparency of our monitoring through six independent sampling and analysis campaigns each year under the Additional Measures framework. Two have taken place since the June Board, and a further campaign is under way this week. Sampling is conducted by experts from the Agency's laboratories, from the ALMERA network and from Japan, including experts from China, the Republic of Korea and the Russian Federation. In this way, international laboratories become co-producers of the data rather than recipients of it.

In June, I travelled to Japan to participate personally in seawater sampling for the second time, joining scientists from China, the Republic of Korea and Switzerland, together with Agency experts, to collect samples near the Fukushima Daiichi site, close to the discharge outlet. Transparency of this kind is what builds confidence in continued nuclear safety.

Mr Chairperson,

Today, 417 nuclear power reactors are in operation in 31 countries, comprising more than 379 gigawatts of installed capacity and providing about 9 per cent of the world's total electricity generation. Seventy-eight reactors totalling more than 81 gigawatts of installed capacity are under construction in 17 countries, 3 of which are newcomers. You will find this data on our Power Reactor Information System (PRIS) website, which has just been modernized.

The Agency is supporting 43 countries embarking on nuclear power through the Milestones Approach, while another 20 are considering it.

The *International Ministerial Conference on Nuclear Power*, hosted by the Republic of Korea in Incheon from 27 to 29 October, will bring together ministers, policymakers, industry and other stakeholders to discuss growing demand, energy security and sustainable development. I encourage Member States to register their delegations.

From 1 to 2 December here in Vienna, we will host the *International Symposium on Nuclear Energy R&D: Advancements and Trends 2026*, offering a platform where stakeholders from industry, research institutions, government, regulatory bodies and academia can exchange information on ongoing R&D activities, identify priorities and gaps, and explore opportunities for enhanced cooperation.

We are organizing the third high level meeting of the World Fusion Energy Group (WFEG), here in Vienna on 12 November 2026. Building on the previous two successful meetings, the Group will review achievements and continue playing its catalytic role in helping to accelerate research, development, demonstration, and deployment of fusion energy.

The Agency continues to ensure that nuclear energy and nuclear science are represented in global climate discussions, including with our Atoms4Climate pavilion at the upcoming UN Climate Change Conference, COP31.

When it comes to increasing nuclear energy capacity, access to financing remains a principal challenge, particularly in emerging and developing economies. This is why the IAEA’s partnership with the World Bank Group is such an important step forward. On 14 July, during the United Nations High-Level Political Forum in New York, the Agency and the Bank co-organized a high-level side event on unlocking capital for clean energy. It explored how international financial institutions can support Member States choosing nuclear energy to meet their development and energy security needs.

The Agency continues to broaden its engagement with international financial institutions and multilateral development banks, moving from high-level dialogue towards practical cooperation and capacity building. Most recently, in August, the IAEA hosted a three-day capacity building workshop in Vienna bringing together representatives of several IFIs to deepen their understanding of nuclear power programmes, including the IAEA Milestones Approach, nuclear infrastructure, safety, legal and regulatory frameworks, financing readiness and other considerations relevant to potential nuclear energy investments. These continued engagements are helping to build the institutional understanding needed for IFIs to assess nuclear energy projects and, ultimately, to expand financing options available to Member States.

To strengthen energy security and reliability, most countries with mature nuclear fleets are already extending, or preparing to extend, their operation beyond their originally envisaged lifetimes. In December, Japan will host in Tokyo the *Agency's Sixth International Conference on Nuclear Power Plant Life Management*, facilitating exchanges on practices, innovations and regulatory approaches for safe, sustainable and efficient long-term operation.

The Nuclear Harmonization and Standardization Initiative continues its work towards the safe and timely deployment of small modular reactors and other advanced reactors.

In August in Washington, DC, I launched ATLAS (Atomic Technologies Licensed for Applications at Sea) with the United States as our host. The ministerial event brought together 650 participants representing Member States, industry, non-governmental organizations and other stakeholders and outlined our efforts.

International interest in ATLAS is substantial, and we are launching at precisely the right time. By bringing together the nuclear and maritime sectors, we have the opportunity to shape the future of two crucial industries — energy and shipping — and to build global confidence in the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear technology at sea.

In liaison with the International Maritime Organization, we will create a framework promoting and supporting the safe and secure development and deployment of peaceful nuclear applications at sea, specifically floating nuclear power plants and nuclear-powered ships. ATLAS will help to clarify issues related to applicable legal frameworks and instruments, promote efficiency in the licensing of these technologies, and enable nuclear and maritime regulators and other stakeholders to inform changes, if necessary, to their requirements and regulatory practices. It will also enhance the Agency's ability to implement efficient and effective safeguards for peaceful nuclear applications at sea, allowing the development of this technology to proceed expeditiously. I encourage interested Member States and relevant stakeholders to participate in the ATLAS dialogue over the coming months as we begin the implementation stage of this exciting initiative.

Looking ahead, every segment of the front end of the nuclear fuel cycle will need to respond to rising demand. From 13-15 October in Vienna, the Agency will hold the *International Conference on Fuel Supply Chain for Sustainable Nuclear Power Development*, examining achievements, challenges and requirements across the fuel supply chain, including those associated with small modular reactors and other advanced technologies. I encourage Member States to participate.

Mr Chairperson,

Since its inception, the Marie Sklodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme (MSCFP) has made a real contribution in widening access to the nuclear field and bolstering the workforce of tomorrow. Across six application cycles, it has selected 860 students from 135 Member States. Of the 561 graduates, 236 have secured IAEA-facilitated internships, while others have pursued doctoral studies or employment in the field. The seventh call opened on 1 September. Continued extrabudgetary contributions are essential to sustain the programme.

Since 2023, the Lise Meitner Programme (LMP) has organized eight visits hosted by seven Member States, reaching 115 professionals from 49 countries. Its latest programme, hosted by the Rosatom Technical Academy and JINR in August 2026, covered the nuclear power lifecycle, fuel cycle, safety, security, safeguards and research and development. Three further visits are scheduled in China, France and Austria in 2026. I would like to request additional hosts to come forward so that we can expand the programme from 2027 onward.

Mr Chairperson,

Since the last Board of Governors meeting in June, a few large payments have been made, and the Agency’s liquidity situation has improved. However, the Agency’s financial stability and continuity of operations depend on the timely payment of assessed contributions. As a number of contributions for 2026 are still outstanding, I would like to urge all Member States to settle any outstanding contributions as soon as possible.

In closing, I want to thank Member States for their continued engagement and support. At a time of conflict and fragmentation, the Agency's role in the pursuit of peace, security and development is more necessary than ever, and I am confident that I can continue to count on your steadfast support.

1. This report has been produced for the 70th regular session (2026) of the General Conference in
response to resolution GC(69)/RES/7, in which the General Conference requested the Director General
to report in detail on implementation of the resolution and on other relevant developments in the
intervening period. This report covers the period from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026. 1
2. The Agency continued its efforts to maintain and strengthen nuclear, radiation, transport and
waste safety, and emergency preparedness and response (EPR) capabilities, focusing, inter alia, on the
technical areas and geographical regions where the need for such efforts is greatest. The Agency
implemented numerous activities and services to assist Member States considering or planning for the
introduction of nuclear power or radiation technology; establishing or strengthening their safety

and radiation safety, including with regard to emerging technologies. 2
3. The Agency continued to encourage and support Member States to become Contracting Parties
to the Convention on Nuclear Safety (CNS), the Joint Convention on the Safety of Spent Fuel
Management and on the Safety of Radioactive Waste Management (Joint Convention), and States
Parties to the Convention on Early Notification of a Nuclear Accident (Early Notification Convention)
and the Convention on Assistance in the Case of a Nuclear Accident or Radiological Emergency
(Assistance Convention). Activities related to the Conventions are reported in detail in subsequent
sections of this report. 3
4. In March 2026, a report by the Director General containing the draft Nuclear Safety Review 202 6
was submitted to the Board of Governors. The final version of the Nuclear Safety Review 2026, prepared
in the light of discussions at the Board of Governors, is provided as an information document at the 70 th
regular session of the General Conference. The Nuclear Safety Review 202 6 provides an overview of
the status, trends and related past and planned Agency activities in the area of nuclear, radiation,
transport and waste safety, as well as EPR . It also presents priorities identified by the Agency and
addressed in the Agency’s Programme and Budget, including outcomes, outputs, timelines and
performance indicators. 4
5. The Agency held the seventh International Conference on Effective Nuclear and Radiation
Regulatory Systems: Strengthening Competence, Agility and Connection in the Modern Era
(RegCon2026), convening 349participants from 104 Member States and 11 organizations in Vienna in
April 2026. Participants explored three key shifts: moving beyond a traditional focus on technical
expertise towards a more holistic approach to competence, integrating leadership development,
organisational culture, and workforce sustainability; strengthening agility through resilience,
emphasizing anticipation, preparedness and recovery, whilemaintaining robust nuclear and radiation
safety and security objectives; and reinforcing connection through stronger regional and international
networks as practical mechanisms for cooperation, trust-buildingand the shared use of resources. The
key messages from RegCon2026 will be sustained beyond the conference: carried forward both in time
through future international and regional conferences and institutional processes, as well as outward
across organizations and regions. A conference report is under development. 5
6. The International Nuclear Safety Advisory Group (INSAG) marked 40 years of advancing nuclear
safety in 2025 and met in Vienna in November 2025 and in April 2026. INSAG formed subgroups to
work on priority areas identified from its nuclear landscape strategic planning and continued to develop
new publications that address the current and emerging nuclear and radiation safety landscape. 6
