7. The Agency continued to provide assistance through its legislative assistance programme,
supporting the establishment and strengthening of comprehensive national nuclear legal frameworks
implementing the relevant instruments and building the capacity of officials in nuclear law. During the
reporting period, the Agency conducted, upon request, 11 reviews of draft and enacted nuclear
legislation, reflecting Member States’ commitment to establishing and strengthening their national
nuclear legal frameworks. The Member States receiving this support were Armenia, Colombia, El
Salvador, Liberia, the Philippines, Saint Lucia, Seychelles, Thailand (two reviews), Turkmenistan and
Uzbekistan, with country- specific bilateral legislative assistance provided through written comments
and advice on drafting national nuclear legislation. The Agency conducted 13 bilateral legislative
activities consisting of 10 awareness raising meetings for decision makers, policymakers, senior officials
and parliamentarians, and 3 national workshops on international and national nuclear law. Under the
framework of the legislative assistance programme, the Agency also trained six fellows in nuclear law,
five through the technical cooperation programme and one through the IAEA Marie-Skłodowska-Curie
Fellowship Programme. 7
8. The Agency served as the secretariat of the 26th Meeting of the International Expert Group on
Nuclear Liability (INLEX) in Vienna in May 2026. The Group discussed the most recent developments
in the field of nuclear liability, including national aspects and the implementation of international legal
instruments. Further, the Group discussed liability issues regarding small modular reactors (SMRs), the
geographical scope of the 2004 Paris Convention, the 1963 and 1997 Vienna Conventions on Civil
Liability for Nuclear Damage, the Convention on Supplementary Compensation for Nuclear Damage
(CSC) and the treatment of non- nuclear States, and the c urrent liability limits of the Parties to the 1963
Vienna Convention. INLEX also discussed the Amendment to the CSC , as well as nuclear damage
compensation by a State Party to the 2004 Paris Convention, the Brussels Convention Supplementary
to the Paris Convention on Third Party Liability in the Field of Nuclear Energy and the CSC. The Group
also discussed the update of th e explanatory texts on the nuclear liability instruments adopted under the
Agency’s auspices in 1997 and the one on the Joint Protocol Relating to the Application of the Vienna
Convention and the Paris Convention. 8

15. The Agency held a Technical Meeting on the Generic RoadMap for Establishing the Nuclear
Safety Infrastructure for a First Nuclear Reactor in Vienna in September 2025. The Generic RoadMap
(GRM) project meetings provided strategic planning tools and practical guidance for sequential
infrastructure development. Informational publications, training materials and a common platform were
further developed under the GRM project throughout 2025. Although the project formally concluded at
the end of the year, remaining actions, including the issuance of publications such as the GRM Safety
Report, continued into 2026. 15
16. The Agency continued to assist Member States, upon request, in implementing and optimizing
the use of the regulatory data system, now known as the Regulatory Authority Information System
(RAIS+). Support is provided through remote assistance, expert missions, regional workshops and the
provision of RAIS+ servers. A train the trainers workshop was held in Vienna in December 2025 to
increase the pool of RAIS+ experts able to support Member States. A Technical M eeting to Share
Experience and Feedback on the Use of the Regulatory Authority Information System (RAIS+) was
organized in Vienna in May 2026 in order to gather users’ feedback on RAIS+ and plan further
updates. 16
17. During the reporting period, the Agency continued to explore the use of artificial intelligence (AI)
in safety-significant applications, including design safety and radiation protection, as well as in training
and report analysis. The Agency developed a roadmap to integrate AI and emerging digital technologies
into safety-related document processing, including in retrieving technical data and checking the
compliance of safety data with requirements, thereby identifying gaps and best practices. 17
18. The Agency organized an International Symposium on Artificial Intelligence and Nuclear Energy,
held in Vienna in December 2025 to explore a broad range of topics, including regulatory considerations
and the important role of early regulatory engagement in integrating AI into nuclear technologies. The
event gathered 553 participants from 72 Member States and 12 non -governmental and
intergovernmental o rganizations, as well as over 1000 online participants. 18

More Linux desktop users means companies can’t as easily ignore Linux users. For example, better hardware and software support. There is also higher potential for more user donations to open source projects.

Though, more users are also means more problems. Security through obscurity becomes harder to justify. For example, the AUR has been infested recently with malware.

Linux, with its love for free and open source licenses that allow quick forks, is difficult (not impossible) to control. Due to lack of users, many companies and governments don’t even bother trying to control Linux users since the effort isn’t worth it. For example, the US carved out an age verification exception for Linux and other open source OS’s. The thought process probably entailed that its mostly professionals and nerds using Linux anyway, not kids. Similarly, Brave gave out Brave Origin for free on Linux. Brave explicitly said they did it because they expected the Linux community to fork it if they didn’t (some desktops that ship Brave apparently already had created a Brave Origin like experience according to Brave). Considering the small percentage of Linux users, it’s easier to just focus on making money on other platforms and let Linux users be the loud tech spokespersons for their friends, family, and colleagues on other platforms.

I hope you’re right, but I’m afraid you aren’t.

Linux gaining (a little bit) of traction over the last decade made so many new distributions come out. It’s like fast fashion, like every user wants to express who they are through their distinct OS.

Alas, maintaining seriously a distribution in terms of security is a very hard and tedious job. Arch decided not to do it and openly leaves it to the users. RedHat/Fedora and SuSE have big resources and do it seriously, Debian does it somewhat and Ubuntu so-so.

But all the derivative are often from a small group of friends’ initiative or from small structures who cannot pay full-time security engineers to check every package update, to update SELinux profiles and run the tests… So derivatives are, at best, as secure as their parent distro, and usually worse.

So it seems more users entails more scattering, which entails less security in general.
